image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Annotated geographic forecast map / path map**
- It overlays a **storm track line**, **uncertainty circles**, and a **cone of uncertainty** on a map.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **No faceting or small multiples**
- **Layered overlay** on a single map:
  - multiple forecast paths drawn together
  - circles placed along the forecast track
  - a shaded cone formed by connecting the circles
  - annotation callouts with numbered labels

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (longitude/latitude) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map |
| Storm forecast path (N.H.C. path) | Ordered spatial sequence | Black line path across map |
| Forecast points along path | Ordered spatial sequence | Pink points positioned on map |
| Forecast uncertainty | Quantitative | Circle size/area (larger circles) |
| Forecast lead time / progression along path | Ordinal / temporal sequence | Order of points/circles along the path from south to north |
| Different organizations’ forecasts | Categorical/nominal | Multiple dashed gray path lines |
| Cone of uncertainty extent | Quantitative / spatial region | Light shaded cone area |
| Broader storm impact area / weather extent | Quantitative / spatial region | Larger semi-transparent pink shaded area |
| Annotation step number (1–6) | Ordinal | Numbered black callout markers |
| Place names / region names | Categorical/nominal | Text labels on map |

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  Love the catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the map:  “Hulking Hurricane” by Ms. Hogan’s Period 7 class at Brooklyn Tech HS, “Predictions for Hurricane XYZ” by Grace R. of the Academy of Saint Elizabeth, and “Ripping and Roaring, Hurricane Soaring” by Sydney of Comet's class at Hanover-Horton HS.

Just a few notes for all. 

The hurricane forecast cone is a sample cone and not the cone for Dorian.   The article that included the map was published as Dorian was approaching the Bahamas.  (We will give you access to the article in tomorrow afternoon’s Reveal.) 

To learn more about the cone, go to this National Hurricane Center video (https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/cone_usage.php) with two of their meteorologists explaining many of the misunderstandings about what the hurricane forecast cone says and does not say.  They should be given an award for explaining this otherwise deceptively simple graph. 

To learn more about the probability model that is used to construct the cone, go to www.hnc.noaa.gov/aboutcone.shtml.  (1 of 2)

comments.raw_comment: After studying the graph, the first thing that jumped out to me was the direction of the map, as it moves from inland to the sea, starting at 1 and ending at 5; a hurricane comes from the ocean to the mainland and follows the opposite path depicted in the graph. Therefore, the map cannot be a path of the movement of the hurricane. In addition, the fact that point 1, "different organizations make their forecasts", was outside of a circle and not even in the "cone" where the other circles are led me to the conclusion that this is probably because the different organizations (that may not be weather-related) may not have made valid hurricane predictions. After tracing the other circles, it appears that the smaller circles are more accurate, or they have more certainty regarding the hurricane.

After tracing the other circles, it appears that the smaller circles are more accurate, or they have more certainty regarding the hurricane.

Headline: Hurricane Dorian... More Like Hurricane Scorpion

I noticed that there is one pink outline and inside of that is a cone, which is made up of circles. The larger the circle the more misgiving the prediction can be. As the storm goes on, the hurricane becomes more unpredictable. The dotted lines throughout the graph symbolize different organizations' predictions of the hurricane and where it will hit. The hurricane could take place anywhere inside the cone, but it can also take place outside within the pink outlining. Also, the line inside the cones and circles symbolizes the storms estimated path. Lastly, I noticed that the majority of the hurricane takes place on land, instead of water.

I wonder how the N.H.C. made the calculations and estimations to create their predictions? How long did it take to collect the data? Did they use previous storms and patterns to create their predictions? Why were cones and circles used to illustrate the pathway of the storm? Did they focus more on the land because they wanted people to evacuate and be safe? What are the chances of the hurricane hitting at one of the other organizations' predictions?

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  Love the catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the map:  “Hulking Hurricane” by Ms. Hogan’s Period 7 class at Brooklyn Tech HS, “Predictions for Hurricane XYZ” by Grace R. of the Academy of Saint Elizabeth, and “Ripping and Roaring, Hurricane Soaring” by Sydney of Comet's class at Hanover-Horton HS.

Just a few notes for all. 

The hurricane forecast cone is a sample cone and not the cone for Dorian.   The article that included the map was published as Dorian was approaching the Bahamas.  (We will give you access to the article in tomorrow afternoon’s Reveal.) 

To learn more about the cone, go to this National Hurricane Center video (https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/cone_usage.php) with two of their meteorologists explaining many of the misunderstandings about what the hurricane forecast cone says and does not say.  They should be given an award for explaining this otherwise deceptively simple graph. 

To learn more about the probability model that is used to construct the cone, go to www.hnc.noaa.gov/aboutcone.shtml.  (1 of 2)

comments.raw_comment: After studying the graph, the first thing that jumped out to me was the direction of the map, as it moves from inland to the sea, starting at 1 and ending at 5; a hurricane comes from the ocean to the mainland and follows the opposite path depicted in the graph. Therefore, the map cannot be a path of the movement of the hurricane. In addition, the fact that point 1, "different organizations make their forecasts", was outside of a circle and not even in the "cone" where the other circles are led me to the conclusion that this is probably because the different organizations (that may not be weather-related) may not have made valid hurricane predictions. After tracing the other circles, it appears that the smaller circles are more accurate, or they have more certainty regarding the hurricane.

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  Love the catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the map:  “Hulking Hurricane” by Ms. Hogan’s Period 7 class at Brooklyn Tech HS, “Predictions for Hurricane XYZ” by Grace R. of the Academy of Saint Elizabeth, and “Ripping and Roaring, Hurricane Soaring” by Sydney of Comet's class at Hanover-Horton HS.

Just a few notes for all. 

The hurricane forecast cone is a sample cone and not the cone for Dorian.   The article that included the map was published as Dorian was approaching the Bahamas.  (We will give you access to the article in tomorrow afternoon’s Reveal.) 

To learn more about the cone, go to this National Hurricane Center video (https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/cone_usage.php) with two of their meteorologists explaining many of the misunderstandings about what the hurricane forecast cone says and does not say.  They should be given an award for explaining this otherwise deceptively simple graph. 

To learn more about the probability model that is used to construct the cone, go to www.hnc.noaa.gov/aboutcone.shtml.  (1 of 2)

comments.raw_comment: After studying the graph, the first thing that jumped out to me was the direction of the map, as it moves from inland to the sea, starting at 1 and ending at 5; a hurricane comes from the ocean to the mainland and follows the opposite path depicted in the graph. In addition, the fact that point 1, "different organizations make their forecasts", was outside of a circle and not even in the "cone" where the other circles are led me to the conclusion that this is probably because the different organizations (that may not be weather-related) may not have made valid hurricane predictions. After tracing the other circles, it appears that the smaller circles are more accurate, or they have more certainty regarding the hurricane.

Thanks to all students who responded.  Love the catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the map:  “Hulking Hurricane” by Ms. Hogan’s Period 7 class at Brooklyn Tech HS, “Predictions for Hurricane XYZ” by Grace R. of the Academy of Saint Elizabeth, and “Ripping and Roaring, Hurricane Soaring” by Sydney of Comet's class at Hanover-Horton HS.

Just a few notes for all. 

The hurricane forecast cone is a sample cone and not the cone for Dorian.   The article that included the map was published as Dorian was approaching the Bahamas.  (We will give you access to the article in tomorrow afternoon’s Reveal.) 

To learn more about the cone, go to this National Hurricane Center video (https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/cone_usage.php) with two of their meteorologists explaining many of the misunderstandings about what the hurricane forecast cone says and does not say.  They should be given an award for explaining this otherwise deceptively simple graph. 

To learn more about the probability model that is used to construct the cone, go to www.hnc.noaa.gov/aboutcone.shtml.  (1 of 2)

comments.raw_comment: After studying the graph, the first thing that jumped out to me was the direction of the map, as it moves from inland to the sea, starting at 1 and ending at 5; a hurricane comes from the ocean to the mainland and follows the opposite path depicted in the graph. Therefore, the map cannot be a path of the movement of the hurricane. In addition, the fact that point 1, "different organizations make their forecasts", was outside of a circle and not even in the "cone" where the other circles are led me to the conclusion that this is probably because the different organizations (that may not be weather-related) may not have made valid hurricane predictions. After tracing the other circles, it appears that the smaller circles are more accurate, or they have more certainty regarding the hurricane.

Also, the line inside the cones and circles symbolizes the storms estimated path. Lastly, I noticed that the majority of the hurricane takes place on land, instead of water.

I wonder how the N.H.C. made the calculations and estimations to create their predictions? How long did it take to collect the data? Did they use previous storms and patterns to create their predictions? Why were cones and circles used to illustrate the pathway of the storm? Did they focus more on the land because they wanted people to evacuate and be safe? What are the chances of the hurricane hitting at one of the other organizations' predictions?
